2207.prule: Right-to-left moraic trochees over the stress domain: primary stress on the final syllable if it is closed (CVC = heavy; the language has no CVV), otherwise on the penult. In citation forms each word is its own prosodic phrase, so the rule reads as final-if-heavy-else-penult at word level; in connected speech the same parse runs from the right edge of the prosodic phrase (~Intonation Unit), so individual words' stress shifts with phrasal context.
2207.srule: Secondary stress on every second syllable counting leftward from the primary stress (right-to-left moraic trochees); closed (CVC) syllables attract stress and interrupt the alternating count; an optional additional secondary stress on the initial syllable when the second syllable is stressed (clash, 'binary plus clash'), found in about a third of eligible wordlist tokens but mostly avoided in discourse.

2208.prule: Primary stress on the final syllable of the word, quantity-insensitive. Payne & Payne 2013: 'Primary stress in Panare is phonetically associated with raised pitch and increased intensity. It most often occurs on the final syllable of a word'; '... words contain final primary stress' (kïrïnïpén 'dog', yutën 'goes', yamayáj, yamañé); the orthography leaves final stress unwritten and marks stress only 'when it occurs anywhere other than the last syllable of a word'. Exceptions: 'A few stems in Panare have lexically-marked stress on the penultimate syllable' (no minimal pairs: yompíku 'scold', yuwarupúta) and grammatically conditioned leftward shifts of primary stress on verbs with a direct object or dative ('grammatical' stress). Cauty 1978 ('the stress may be on any syllable of the word'; two speakers, 1,400 words, no minimal pairs) is the earlier preliminary description and states no rule; Meira 2006: 201 'usually penultimate' is a lone second-hand dissent.

tn.quote: Le geviya possède un système à schèmes tonals et de ce fait économique, le domaine des tons n’étant pas la syllabe mais le mot (phonologique). Les profils de surface se ramènent fondamentalement à quatre schèmes et donc à autant de catégories tonales pour les noms (/H/, /HB/, /B/ et /BH/). Pour les verbes le nombre de catégories s’élève à deux (/H/ et /B/). ... Une autre caractéristique du système est l’évitement des tons modulés et des abaissements tonals non automatiques (downstep).
tn.translation: Geviya has a tone-melody (tone-pattern) system, hence an economical one, the domain of the tones being not the syllable but the (phonological) word. The surface profiles reduce basically to four melodies and thus to as many tonal categories for nouns (/H/, /HL/, /L/ and /LH/). For verbs the number of categories is two (/H/ and /L/). ... Another characteristic of the system is the avoidance of contour tones and of non-automatic tonal lowerings (downstep).

2215.prule: A dynamic (stress) accent, explicitly distinguished from tone, falls on the stem (root) syllable of the word — on the first stem syllable if the stem is disyllabic — so prefixes (noun-class, pronominal, e.g. a- in afogólo 'hat') are unstressed and stress position is set by morphological structure, not by syllable count or weight; in verbs it moves to the final syllable in the unshortened imperative (Heepe). Nekes 1911 gives the same default ('In der Regel ist die erste Stammsilbe akzentuiert') and states it is independent of tone height.

2215.tone: Ewondo is a register tone language: Heepe 1919: 'Jede Silbe hat ihre Tonhöhe, nämlich hoch oder tief'; Nekes 1911 §16 marks five practical tones. Both authors insist the dynamic accent (Starkton) is a separate, weak system independent of tone: Nekes §15 'Alle Töne, ob Hoch-, Tief- oder Mittelton, können den dynamischen Akzent haben'; §19 afogólo has stress on the low-toned 2nd syllable, not the high-toned 3rd. Heepe's kymograms show the Starkton raising the pitch of low-toned stem-initial syllables (manu, mabo, Zoo-lana) and advises learners to ignore stress at first. Redden 1979 (modern grammar, one Yaoundé speaker) posits 3 tones + 3 junctures as the only suprasegmentals and makes no stress statement; Pichon 1950 and Nekes 1913 are likewise silent (Nekes 1913 p. 7 only mentions reduction of an unaccented final vowel).

2216.heavy: Light = CV (one mora); heavy = CVː, CVC (two morae: long vowel = two morae, coda = extra mora); superheavy = CVːC, CVCC (no more than one per word; CVCC only word-finally with 1SG /-t/). Word-final codas do not count for weight, so a final CVC syllable is light ([ˈʔig.bil]) while a final CVːC counts as heavy by its long vowel ([ta.ˈfuːz]).
2216.prule: Weight-sensitive: stress the heaviest syllable of the word. A superheavy syllable (CVːC, CVCC; at most one per word) is stressed if present; otherwise the LEFTMOST heavy syllable (CVː anywhere, CVC non-finally, since word-final codas do not count for weight); if the word has no heavy syllable, the penult ([ka.ˈsa.fan] 'eclipsed'). 2217.dq: En fang ntúmú, l’accent remplit donc une fonction démarcative en ce sens qu’il permet d’identifier non seulement la limite du préfixe nominal, mais également la première syllabe de la base.
2217.prule: Accent always on the first syllable of the base (root, or nominal / verbo-nominal stem); the noun-class prefix is unaccented and is followed by a slight pause, so the accent is demarcative of the prefix-stem boundary. Position is anchored to the morphological stem, not counted from a word edge. Overlaid on a two- or three-register tone system (haut, moyen, bas).
2217.srule: Not mentioned in Ollomo Ella 2012 (whole article read, accent passages §6, §§24-27, §34): the source names a single accent per nominal, on the base-initial syllable, and says nothing about secondary or rhythmic accent; all accent examples have monosyllabic bases.
2217.quote: [§6] Le fang ntúmú est une langue tonale à deux ou trois registres (haut, moyen, bas), et accentuelle sur la première syllabe de la base (racine ou thème nominal). ... [§24] Nous avons vu plus haut que le fang ntúmú est à la fois tonale et accentuel. Nous constatons que les locuteurs marquent toujours une légère pause après le préfixe nominal. ... [§25] Nous constatons en outre que la première syllabe de la base (thème ou racine verbo-nominale) est toujours accentuée. En fait pause et accent sont étroitement liés. Exemples: 7) A’kɔ́ Ɂ ‘’pierre’’ | à-kɔ́ Ɂ| /PN5-pierre/ Mə̀ ’kɔ́ Ɂ ‘’pierres’’ …
2217.idn: ntúmú (Ntumu), one of the five Fang dialects (ntumu, okak, mvɛ́ɲ, nzaman, atsi); Guthrie A75A (a named variety of the language); data: Data collected in 1997 in south Cameroon, locality of Mvi-Mangale, by Marie Françoise Rombi; Ntumu speakers located in north Gabon, south Cameroon and Equatorial Guinea
2217.exq_: Nous constatons en outre que la première syllabe de la base (thème ou racine verbo-nominale) est toujours accentuée.
2217.tone: Source calls Fang ntúmú a tone language with two or three registers (haut, moyen, bas) and, at the same time, accentual. Tone is marked on every syllable of the examples (prefixes à-, mə̀-, ò- all low; stems kɔ́Ɂ high, kɔ̀p low) and the accent falls on the stem-initial syllable whether its tone is high (kɔ́Ɂ) or low (kɔ̀p), so accent placement is independent of tone. The dedicated phonologies held for other Fang dialects (Eko 1974; Medjo Mvé 1993, 1997; Zribi-Hertz & Ondo Obame 2022; Bibang Oyee 1990) describe only the tone system and are silent on accent.

tn.quote: Le fang ntúmú est une langue tonale à deux ou trois registres (haut, moyen, bas), et accentuelle sur la première syllabe de la base (racine ou thème nominal). ... La nasale initiale des nominaux problématiques joue effectivement le rôle de préfixe nominal. Elle est syllabique et porte un ton bas ... Au pluriel en revanche, la nasale n’est ni syllabique, ni porteuse d’un ton bas. ... Nous avons vu plus haut que le fang ntúmú est à la fois tonale et accentuel. ... Nous constatons en outre que la première syllabe de la base (thème ou racine verbo-nominale) est toujours accentuée.
tn.translation: Fang Ntumu is a tone language with two or three registers (high, mid, low), and accentual on the first syllable of the base (root or nominal stem). ... The initial nasal of the problematic nominals does play the role of noun prefix. It is syllabic and carries a low tone ... In the plural, by contrast, the nasal is neither syllabic nor the bearer of a low tone. ... We saw above that Fang Ntumu is both tonal and accentual. ... We further observe that the first syllable of the base (stem or verbo-nominal root) is always accented.

2218.dq: Cet accent marque automatiquement la première syllabe du mot phonologique sauf s'il s'agit d'un pronom ou d'une particule grammaticale.
2218.dloc: §4.7.2 « L'accent d'intensité », p. 82; same rule restated in Niggli & Niggli 2007, Esquisse grammaticale du ninkãrɛ (Cahiers No. 11), §1.3.3, p. 26
2218.prule: Non-distinctive intensity stress falls automatically on the first syllable of the phonological word (every lexical word: nouns, verbs...); pronouns and grammatical particles are unstressed. quantity-insensitive, position fixed by the left word edge; the stressed syllable's tone is realised in a raised register (B+ / H+).
2218.srule: None: one accent per word — 'Un mot se compose toujours d'une ou de plusieurs syllabes, l'une étant plus prééminente, les autres étant marginales. La syllabe accentuée constitue le noyau du mot phonologique' (Niggli & Niggli 2007, Esquisse §1.3, p. 24); the phonology volume (§4.7.2, p. 82) marks one intensity accent per lexical word and mentions no secondary or rhythmic stress.
2218.quote: Certains segments sont accentués, ils ont l'accent d'intensité [']. Ces segments d'énoncé sont réalisés avec une intensité particulière sans que l'on puisse attribuer cette intensité à un effet d'insistance. 'Bʋraa la 'sɛ̃ŋɛ la 'Poogo. «L'homme est allé à Pô.» En ninkãrɛ, la place de l'accent d'intensité n'a aucune valeur distinctive. Cet accent marque automatiquement la première syllabe du mot phonologique sauf s'il s'agit d'un pronom ou d'une particule grammaticale. A 'sɛŋɛ la 'Poogo. «Il est allé à Pô.» L'accent d'intensité provoque un rehaussement du niveau mélodique du ton affectant la s…
2218.loc: §4.7.2 « L'accent d'intensité », p. 82; same rule restated in Niggli & Niggli 2007, Esquisse grammaticale du ninkãrɛ (Cahiers No. 11), §1.3.3, p. 26
2218.idn: le ninkãrɛ — the single Burkina Faso 'parler' of gurenne / frafra (gʋrnɛ, nankana); written standard = 'le langage de Guélwongo' (Esquisse: 'C'est le parler de la région Zecco / Guélwongo qui a été retenu pour l'étude présente') (a named variety of the language); data: most data collected January 1996 – August 1998…
2218.exq_: sauf s'il s'agit d'un pronom ou d'une particule grammaticale (examples: subject pronoun A and determiner/particle la carry no stress mark: A 'sɛŋɛ la 'Poogo; 'Bʋraa la 'sɛ̃ŋɛ la 'Poogo)
2218.tone: Ninkãrɛ is a two-tone terraced-level tone language (§4.1, p. 67: 'Le ninkãrɛ ne comporte que deux tonèmes; le ton haut... subissant un abaissement (ou down-step), et le ton bas'); the intensity accent is listed there (with intonation) among the causes of tone-height modification. Stress is thus an automatic, non-contrastive overlay on the lexical tone, marked only by raised register of the stressed syllable's tone; tone, not stress, is the contrastive prosody (§4.8 notes tone's low functional load).

tn.quote: Selon nos analyses le ninkãrɛ appartient au type des langues au système tonal en terrasse ou en paliers. Le ninkãrɛ ne comporte que deux tonèmes; - le ton haut (a^), dans certains contextes toniques, subissant un abaissement (ou down-step), - et le ton bas (a_). Dans la chaîne parlée, les tons subissent des modifications selon leur contexte tonique. Ces modifications peuvent être dues à plusieurs causes: • l'intonation • l'accent d'intensité • contexte tonal immédiat Donc, on a deux tons pertinents: ton haut et ton bas, mais plusieurs registres tonétiques.
tn.translation: According to our analyses Ninkãrɛ belongs to the type of languages with a terraced (stepped) tone system. Ninkãrɛ has only two tonemes: the high tone (á), which in certain tonal contexts undergoes a lowering (down-step), and the low tone (à). In connected speech the tones undergo modifications according to their tonal context. These modifications may be due to several causes: intonation, the intensity accent, the immediate tonal context. So there are two distinctive tones, high and low, but several phonetic registers.
tn.cite: Niggli, Idda & Urs Niggli. 2007. De la phonologie à l'orthographe: Le ninkãrɛ au Burkina Faso. Cahiers de Recherches Linguistiques de la SIL et l'ANTBA Burkina Faso, Numéro 10. Ouagadougou: Société Internationale de Linguistique. 130 pp.
tn.note: Two level tones, high and low, on every syllable, in a terraced system; non-automatic downstep of high after an underlying low; a separate automatic initial intensity accent; low functional load.

2219.dq: There are also two pertinent tones at the word level and nasalization of vowels is contrastive with non-nasalized vowels.
2219.dloc: sec. 2.1 'Pronunciation of vowels, consonants, tone, and nasalization', pp. 12-13; sec. 2.2 tone contrasts, p. 15. (pages read directly)
2219.prule: Word-tone system: two contrastive tones (high, low) 'at the word level'; exactly one syllable per word carries a tone diacritic (acute = high, macron = low), its position is lexically contrastive (sere-H-final 'mountain ridge' vs se-H-re 'sun'), and the pitch of the rest of the word follows from that syllable's tone and position (pre-final H = level high then straight low on the last syllable; final/monosyllabic H = downglide; pre-final L = level low then downglide on the last syllable; final/monosyllabic L = upglide). No stress rule is stated and the word 'stress' does not occur.
2219.srule: Not mentioned in Loeweke & May 1980, sec. 2 Phonology (pp. 12-16 read; 'stress' does not occur anywhere in the grammar, pp. 5-106).
2219.quote: [printed p. 12, sec. 2.1] There are sixteen letters in the alphabet of Fasu (Namo Me) which divide into five vowels and eleven consonants. There are also two pertinent tones at the word level and nasalization of vowels is contrastive with non-nasalized vowels. For more details see May-Loeweke, 1965. [p. 13] In the following list V stands for vowel. High and low tone is marked above the vowel and nasalization is marked below the vowel. V́ high tone on vowels of single syllable words is pronounced as a downglide. V́ high tone on vowels of syllables prior to the last syllable is pronounced as le…
2219.loc: sec. 2.1 'Pronunciation of vowels, consonants, tone, and nasalization', pp. 12-13; sec. 2.2 tone contrasts, p. 15. (pages read directly)
2219.idn: Fasu (Namo Me; alternate spelling Faso; older names Fasu-Kaibu, Kaipu, Namumi, Namomebo), West Kutubuan Family; west of Lake Kutubu, Nipa Sub Province, Southern Highlands Province, PNG; two dialects: Kaipu/Sisipia/Kewotiki villages vs. villages southeast of the Aiyo River (Ririku, Aiyo, Mano, Anuwape, Tamatiki...)…
2219.tone: The 1980 grammar describes tone, not stress: two word-level tones H and L, one tone-marked syllable per word, whole-word melody derived from the marked syllable's tone and its position relative to the last syllable; minimal sets show both the tone value (nómo 'you' / nōmo 'I') and the position of the marked syllable (seré 'mountain ridge' / sére 'sun') are contrastive. The dictionary front matter (May & Loeweke, Fasu (Namo Me) dictionary introduction, pp. 7-8) repeats the same glide descriptions and does not use 'stress'. The authors' own equation of the marked syllable with a 'nuclear' (stressed) syllable is in May & Loeweke 1965 (Anthropological Linguistics 7(5): 89-97), reachable only second-hand: Cahill 2011 (SIL e-WP 2011-008 sec. 2.3) and Hyman 2006 (Phonology 23, who classes Fasu as stress-accent + tone, tone dependent on stress) and Hyman 2009. Cahill notes it 'does not fit the usual pitch-accent type, since the accented syllable may itself exhibit contrastive tone'. Culminative, lexically placed prominence carrying an H/L contrast; no secondary stress mentioned anywhere.

2221.tone: Wurm 1975:494 (phylum survey, explicitly 'a few notes' after J. Rule 1952 and W. M. Rule 1965): 'Suprasegmentals: A two-tone system is present.' Weiner 1988:xvii-xviii (ethnographer reproducing Rule 1977:8-10): 'two tonemes, high and low, that affect only a small number of word pairs', example hae~ 'egg, seed, fruit' vs hae~ [high tone] 'dog'. Rule 1977 (primary, Google Books only, page not shown): the sentence-intonation pattern of Foe is 'for each word of the sentence to follow along on a mid tone sequence (with stressed syllables slightly higher in tone), and for the final terminating contour consisting of a medium high tone falling down to a low tone on the last syllable of the verb expression'; a second excerpt describes the command contour ('the final syllable of the command verb expression to undergo a slight rise from low to mid'). So the primary treats Foe as having stressed syllables whose main correlate is a slight pitch rise, alongside a marginal two-toneme contrast; no stress position is stated in anything reachable. 2222.dq: Mais si l'accentuation proprement dite fait défaut, on rencontre en revanche l'intonation propre à un grand nombre de parlers nègres et qui se fait sentir, non sur les mots, mais sur les phrases.
2222.dloc: Première partie (phonétique), p. 36 (manueldahomengr00delagoog), section 'Accentuation et intonation'
2222.prule: No word stress: 'l'accent tonique n'existe pas en dahoméen'; every syllable of a word has equal weight and all syllables are pronounced recto tono (level). 2222.tone: Delafosse 1894 does not recognise lexical tone (a pre-tonal-analysis manual; 'sur le même ton' refers to level delivery). Modern descriptions opened in the copy consulted treat Fon as a two-toneme /H, L/ language and do not discuss stress: Gbéto 2004 JWAL 31(1) sec. 2.3 (phonetic tones B, H, M, BH, HB, BHB; tonemes /B/ and /H/; 'syllabe accentuée' used only for the French/English source syllable of a loan, mapped to H), Gnanguenon 2014 thèse ch. 6 (two tonemes, following Guédou 1985), Laleye 2016 thèse sec. 1.2 ('langue tonale... deux tons lexicaux, haut et bas'). Second-hand Google Books of Brousseau 2003 (in Plag ed.), saved, read 'Fongbe generates syllables and words fully specified for tones, and phrases bearing stress' and 'Tone determines prominence' — consistent with no lexical word stress and phrase-level prominence. A reviewer may prefer tone or pitch accent on the modern literature; the record is coded from the source actually opened, which denies word stress outright.

tn.quote: Au niveau phonétique, le fon présente les tons suivants: B, H, M, B͡H, H͡B, B͡H͡B. De ces réalisations tonales, seules B et H ont statut de phonèmes: (1) àtá̰ 'salive' / àtà̰ 'vin de palme' tá 'allumer' / tà 'tamiser' ... Les tonèmes /B/ et /H/ connaissent un certain nombre de réalisations phonétiques. Ainsi, le tonème /H/ est réalisé [B͡H] devant consonne voisée. ... tn.translation: At the phonetic level Fon has the following tones: L, H, M, LH, HL, LHL. Of these tonal realisations only L and H have the status of phonemes: (1) àtá̰ 'saliva' / àtà̰ 'palm wine', tá 'light' / tà 'sift' ... The tonemes /L/ and /H/ have a number of phonetic realisations. Thus the toneme /H/ is realised [LH] before (i.e. after, following) a voiced consonant. ... The M tone, for its part, results from the raising of /L/ when the latter occurs before an H tone.
tn.cite: Gbéto, Flavien. 2004. L'expression de la minimalité prosodique dans les emprunts européens en fon. Journal of West African Languages 31(1): 15-31.
tn.note: Two tonemes, H and L (B); M, rising LH, falling HL and LHL are derived realisations (H > LH after a voiced consonant, L > M before H). Silva's Regra 1 / Regra 2: assign stress to the last or to the penultimate syllable of the word.
2223.srule: Secondary stress on alternate syllables counted right-to-left from the lexically placed primary (trochees when the primary is penultimate, iambs when it is final, iterating leftward); a single leftover word-initial syllable also bears secondary stress as a degenerate foot: [ˌwa.ˈpɛ.la] 'livro', [ˌe.tse.ˈka] 'pedaço', [el.ˌtʃo.so.ˈa] 'ovelha', [ˌklɛ.tal.ˈkã.ne] 'cobra venenosa', [ˌso.ˌkʰlo.ko.ˈdõː.kʲa] 'ano', [ˌja.de.ˌdõː.do.ˈa] 'eu era menino'; the same footing in verb citation forms ([ˌkʰlɛtʃaˈka] 'cantar'). 2228.prule: No stress: 'Ударение в Г.я. отсутствует' (stress is absent in Gban). 2228.tone: Explicit denial of stress followed by the tone system (p. 906): four tone levels/registers, four level tonemes (уВ extra-high kpa̋, В high kpá, Н low kpà, уН extra-low kpȁ) and two contour tonemes (уН-уВ rising kpǎ, уН-В mid-rising kpä), illustrated by minimal sets on kpa, ke, gbã, lɛ. Tone-bearing unit is the foot (стопа), mono- or disyllabic (p. 907); on a disyllabic foot a toneme is written as a sequence of two level tones. Tones function as inherent ('lexical'), contextual (tone enclitics, 2.1.3) and grammatical (replacement by extra-low / mid-rising for hesternal and prehesternal perfective; conversion of a verb form into a tone enclitic for imperfective; raising of the preceding tone by two levels for past). Intonation is very limited: neutral level contour with downdrift, a 'comma intonation' with final-vowel lengthening marking non-final clauses, no special interrogative intonation. No accent, pitch-accent, prominence or secondary stress is mentioned in 2.1.1-2.1.4 or 2.2.1 (pp. 904-910).

Widmer 2017 denies any weight condition: 'stress is not sensitive to syllable weight. 2229.prule: Widmer 2017 (reference grammar, instrumental): at the WORD level, polysyllabic words spoken in isolation carry a prominent stress on the first syllable (a trochaic pattern); the main correlate is pitch; stress is not phonemic. At the PHRASE level, words in phrases follow an iambic pattern dictated by phrasal intonation: phrasal stress is borne only by lexical syllables (the stem); a monosyllabic stem is stressed on its single syllable, a polysyllabic stem on its second lexical syllable (a'tcho, ka'katsi); this is explicitly not sensitive to syllable weight (/şans.'pa/ with a closed initial still takes second-syllable phrasal stress). CONFLICTS WITH Sharma 1989 (survey sketch): in disyllables the prominent accent is on the initial syllable if it is closed and on the second syllable if both syllables are open; monosyllables carry a prominent stress; words of 3+ syllables carry 'a secondary accent only' (no prominent accent). Widmer's word-level rule (always initial) and his explicit weight-insensitivity both contradict Sharma's weight-conditioned disyllable rule, and Widmer's ka'katsi 'lamb' contradicts Sharma's accentless /ka-ka-ci/ 'lamb'.
